On The 8 th Of July, 2024
 Writ Petition No. 1400 of 2022
 Maliram Agrawal
 Versus
 Indore Municipal Corporation Indore And Others
Appearance:
Shri A.K.Sethi, learned Senior Counsel along with Shri Che  counsel for the petitioner.
Shri Amol Shrivastava, learned counsel for the respondents  ORDER 1.

By this petition preferred under Article 226 of the Constitution of India the petitioner has challenged the action of the respondents by which they have marked "red ink line" on his house situated at 1/1, Sheelnath Camp, Shankar Kumar Ka Bagicha, Indore as well as on the shutter of the shops situated at the ground floor of the house.

The action of the respondents has been challenged by the petitioner on the ground that prior to the same they have not issued any notice to him nor any of the officers of the respondents have orally informed him as to why such marking of red ink is being done.
On the apprehension that the respondents would demolish the house and shops of the petitioner, the instant petition has been preferred by him.

2. After filing of the petition, a notice dated 14.01.2002 (Annexure P/7) was issued to the petitioner in which it was stated that the road from Bhandari Pool to Kulkarni Ka Bhatta Pool is to be widened as per the Indore Development Plan, 2021 (Master Plan) in which the house/plot of the 2 WP-1400-2022 petitioner is an obstruction.
The petitioner was directed to remove the obstructed portion within a period of 5 days.

It was stated that in lieu of compensation the petitioner would be given additional FAR/EDS.
3.

Upon being noticed the respondents have filed their reply in which it has been stated that task of widening of road from Bhandari bridge to Kulkarni Ka Bhatta bridge as per Indore Master Plan,
2021 by widening the road on part of land which vests in the Corporation under Section 305 of the Act has been taken.
Section 305 vests the area which is falling within the widening of the road with the Corporation.

The Apex Court in Ravindra Ramchandra Waghmare V/s. Indore Municipal Corporation (2017) 1 SCC 667 has already upheld the validity of provisions of Section 305 and has Maliram Agrawal vs Indore Municipal Corporation Indore on 8 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64880640/
1 categorically confirmed that land covered under Section 305 for the purpose of widening of road vests in the Corporation whether the said land is a private property or public property.

4. It has been held by the Apex Court as under :-
"83.

Thus with respect to the compensation, considering more or less similar provisions, a Constitution Bench [State of Gujarat v. ShantilalMangaldas, (1969) 1 SCC 509] of this Court has clearly laid down that as a matter of fact actual compensation has to be determined in the first instance, the value of the total loss or deprivation actually suffered.

entities.text: State of Gujarat v. ShantilalMangaldas, (1969) 1 SCC 509]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It has to be balanced with the other relevant aspects for compensation.
The Act provides for payment of compensation.
The view of the High Court that the principle for determination of compensation has not been specified under Section 212 was also not agreed to by this Court.
This Court has also held that the Land Acquisition Act makes market value at a certain date the basis for determination of compensation.
But there is no one sure way of applying the principle.
As is well known when set back is imposed by the line of the street, the land actually acquired by the Corporation may be in some cases a few square yards or even a few square inches.
Then again the land acquired may be of no significant use to anybody except for the 3 WP-1400-2022 Corporation as a part of the street.
The land acquired may be of different shapes, irregular in contour and often shapeless.
If the principle of willing buyer and willing seller is applied there can possibly be no market at all for the property acquired.
This Court opined that the owner gets full indemnification for the loss or deprivation suffered to the building or other interests in the property.
Involvement of the civil courts in finally determining compensation imports judicial norms.
There is no limitation on the power of the appellate Judge.

Thus this Court held that the provisions contained in Sections 212, 216 and 389 were not violative of the provisions of Section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935 or Article 31 of the Constitution.
The case was remanded by this Court to the High Court for examining infringement of Articles 14 and 19 after laying down the aforesaid propositions.
We have on merits found no violation of Articles 14 and 19 also in the instant cases.

84. It was also submitted that the provisions of Sections 305 and 306 are required to be read down by incorporating the requirement of computation of compensation in the light of the principles laid down under the 2013 Act while correlating it with the provisions of Section 387 of the 1956 Act.

In view of the aforesaid dictum of this Court in Municipal Corpn. of the City of Ahmedabad [Municipal Corpn. of the City of Ahmedabad v. State of Gujarat, (1972) 1 SCC 802] , we find no scope to entertain the submission and the reliance by the appellants on Yogendra Kumar Jaiswal v.
State of Bihar [Yogendra Kumar Jaiswal v. State of Bihar, (2016) 3 SCC 183 : (2016) 2 SCC (Cri) 1] is of no avail.

sentences.text: We find the principles laid down in Sections 305, 306 and 387 are quite reasonable.

Reasonable compensation is payable by the Corporation for building or part thereof excluding the land under proviso to Section 305(1) and compensation for inclusion of land in public street is payable under Section 306(3) of the Act.
We do not find any ground so as to read down the provisions.

We refrain to comment upon the submission with respect to the granting additional FAR is not acceptable to some appellants, as it is not the stage of dealing with compensation how the total indemnification is to be made, whether FAR is acceptable to the appellants or not, cannot be decided at this stage.

It need not be decided at this stage whether they have a right to leave the FAR and claim monetary compensation alone which is to be adjudged by the authorities concerned within the pale of the provisions contained in Sections 305, 306 read with Section 387 of the 1956 Act.
How the compensation is to be worked out at the appropriate stage, is the outcome of the authorities concerned and the job of the arbitrator/District Court, as the case may be.

The appellants are at liberty to raise the question with respect to the adequacy of compensation and how the provision of Section 387 has to be interpreted and what would be the just compensation at the appropriate stage of determination of compensation.

Reliance has been placed on Laxmi Devi v. State of Bihar [Laxmi Devi v. State of Bihar, (2015) 10 SCC 241 : (2016) 1 SCC (Civ) 119] and Rajendra Shankar Shukla v. State of Chhattisgarh [Rajendra Shankar Shukla v. State of Chhattisgarh, (2015) 10 SCC 400] . The decision in Laxmi Devi [Laxmi Devi v. State of Bihar, (2015) 10 SCC 241 : (2016) 1 SCC (Civ) 119] is based on the specific provision contained in Section 10-A of the Land Acquisition Act which requires compensation to be paid in a case where emergency clause has been invoked.

sentences.text:
The Collector is required to tender payment of 80%
of compensation before taking possession of the land.
The said provision is not at all attracted to the 1956 Act.

As compensation is offered after vesting, is quite reasonable procedure as envisaged by Article 300-A of the Constitution of India, at which point of time it is offered would not make the provision confiscatory or repugnant.

The compensation under Section 305 or 306 read with Section 387 is on the happening of certain exigency, and various factors are taken into consideration for determination of compensation is a quite valid procedure.
The Corporation cannot be compelled as per the special scheme of Sections 305, 306 and 387 to offer the compensation before removal and vesting.

Reliance on the decision in K.N. Palsikar [Municipal Corpn., Indore v. K.N. Palsikar, AIR 1969 SC 579] so as to contend that the possession should be taken after payment of compensation is totally misplaced.

The aforesaid question was neither raised nor decided by this Court.
This Court has not laid down any such proposition in K.N. Palsikar [Municipal Corpn., Indore v. K.N. Palsikar, AIR 1969 SC 579] , as canvassed.

87. Reliance has also been placed on a decision of this Court in Bhusawal Municipal Council v.
Nivrutti Ramchandra Phalak [Bhusawal Municipal Council v. Nivrutti Ramchandra Phalak, (2015)
14 SCC 327] in which this Court has considered right to property under Article 300-A and held that such right is a human right and delayed payment of compensation leads to alienation of section of society against the system, further public purpose that is setting up of school, is no justification for Maliram Agrawal vs Indore Municipal Corporation Indore on 8 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64880640/
3 delaying/denying compensation in the garb of undertaking developmental projects, without paying the compensation to the landowner concerned as per the statutory provisions.

sentences.text: It was also submitted that the time period was not prescribed within which compensation was to be paid.

In our opinion,
the appellants have questioned the very notice, initiation of action and when no time-limit is fixed for payment of compensation, it goes without saying that it has to be awarded within a "reasonable time".
Law envisages speedy action without unreasonable delay and that is what is expected of the authorities concerned, in respect of the obligation imposed on them to be discharged.

Due to this,
the provision cannot be struck 5 WP-1400-2022 down as arbitrary nor can it be said to be confiscatory in nature.
We expect that the Corporations concerned would do well while offering the compensation to the appellants as expeditiously as possible that is sufficient to take care of their unfounded fear."

5. Faced with the same the learned counsel for the petitioner has submitted that there has not been any measurement by the respondents of the actual width of the road in front of house of the petitioner.

There has been no measurement of the road as well as the house of the petitioner on the spot, thus it cannot be ascertained as to what is the width of the road and what is the portion of the house/plot of the petitioner which would fall within the area which shall be eventually widened.
It is stated that only a show cause notice was issued to the petitioner and there has not been any demarcation with participation of the petitioner.

To this the learned counsel for the respondents has submitted that a joint inspection by a team of the respondents and other competent authorities shall be conducted with full participation of the petitioner and the measurement of the road as well as the house of the petitioner shall be done and further action shall be taken in the matter only as per the said inspection report.
The said proposal of the counsel for the respondents is acceptable to the counsel for the petitioner.

6. Thus in view of the aforesaid, it is directed that the respondents shall constitute a team which would comprise its senior officers as well as an officer of the Town and Country Planning Department, Indore.
The team will also include such officers as would be required for the purpose of measurement and/or demarcation.
Thereafter a notice would be issued to the petitioner informing him the date and time on which the inspection would be done which would at least be 7 days from the date of issuance of the notice.
On that day and time the road in front of the house of the petitioner and his house/plot shall be measured in his presence and a report as regards the same would be prepared.

Thereafter the respondents shall be free to proceed in the matter as per the report in accordance with law.
7.
With the aforesaid direction, petition stands disposed off.
